items.title: L9: Answer-first structure and signposting
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Communicating and Influencing; GOV.UK writing guidance
items.body: At senior levels, how you structure an answer is itself evidence of Communicating and Influencing. A STAR answer told in strict order can leave the panel waiting two minutes to learn what you actually did. An answer-first structure leads with a one-sentence headline that tells the panel where you are going, then supplies the evidence. For example: 'I turned round a failing complaints process by changing how cases were triaged. The situation was...'. The headline gives the panel a frame for their notes, so they can record each part against the right behaviour as you speak. Signposting does the same inside the answer: 'There were three things I did. First... Second... Third...'. Signposts help a panel member who has stopped writing for a moment to rejoin, and they help you to remember where you are if nerves strike. Keep signposts short and honest; do not promise three points and give two. Close with a one-line landing that ties the result back to the question, such as 'So the change reduced repeat contacts and showed I can improve a service without extra resource'. Avoid ending on 'and that was it', which wastes the last impression. Time matters too: a good rule for a main behaviour answer is roughly two to three minutes, with the Action taking the largest share. Practise speaking in headlines. Many strong candidates also deliberately leave one detail for a probe rather than packing everything in, which makes the conversation more natural and keeps the first answer within time.

questions.prompt: Which opening best illustrates an answer-first approach to a Changing and Improving question?

options.text: 'I have always been someone who likes to improve how things are done in my work.'
'This is quite a long story, so please stop me if it begins to go on too long.'
'I redesigned how our complaints were triaged, which halved repeat contacts. Let me explain how.'
'A few years ago I worked in a busy complaints team that was short of staff at the time.'

questions.hint: The headline states what you did and the result before the detail.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of a headline at the start of an answer?

options.text: It shortens the time the panel needs to score, so they may ask fewer follow-ups
It gives the panel a frame to record each part against the right behaviour
It lets you avoid giving a result because the headline already states the outcome
It signals that the answer will be brief, so the panel can relax their note-taking

questions.hint: Panels note evidence against criteria as they listen.

questions.prompt: You say 'There were three things I did' but only describe two. What is the likely effect?

options.text: It undermines the signpost and makes the answer look unfinished or unplanned
It suggests you are being modest, which panels reward with credit
It shows flexibility, since the panel can add the third point itself
It makes the panel assume the third action and give credit for it anyway

questions.prompt: Which closing line best ties an answer back to the question?

options.text: 'I hope that has answered your question and given you what you needed from it.'
'There is a good deal more I could say about it, but I will stop at that point.'
'And that was really all there was to it, so I will leave it there for now.'
'So the change cut repeat contacts, and it showed I can improve a service without extra resource.'

questions.hint: A landing line reinforces the behaviour asked.

questions.prompt: Roughly how long should a main behaviour answer take?

options.text: Under thirty seconds, so that the panel has time for more questions
Five to six minutes, to make sure every detail of the story is covered
As long as it takes for the panel to stop writing and look up
Two to three minutes, with most of that on the Action

questions.hint: Time discipline is part of Communicating and Influencing.

questions.prompt: Why might a strong candidate deliberately leave one detail out of an answer?

options.text: To keep within time and leave a natural opening for a probe
Because panels penalise answers that include every detail of the story
To avoid mentioning the result, which the panel will otherwise probe
Because details of that kind are never scored by the panel

questions.hint: A held-back detail makes the conversation more natural.

questions.prompt: Which habit most weakens the final impression of an answer?

options.text: Linking the outcome to the question
Pausing before the final sentence
Trailing off with 'and that was it'
Restating the result in one line

questions.prompt: A panel member stops writing for a moment and then looks up. How does signposting help?

options.text: It tells them that you have finished and they should now score
It lets them rejoin the answer at the next numbered point
It forces them to take more notes while you carry on talking
It lets you skip over the Action and go straight to the result

questions.prompt: Which structure best fits a question about influencing a sceptical senior colleague?

options.text: Headline of the outcome, who you needed to persuade and why, your approach in order, the result, and what it shows
The decision that was made, with no account of how you reached it or who you persuaded on the way
A chronological diary of each conversation you had with the colleague, in the order that they happened
The colleague's full career history, a list of the meetings you attended and the final decision made

questions.hint: Structure the evidence to show influence.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with starting 'This is quite a long story, so stop me if it goes on'?

options.text: It makes the answer too short to be scored
It breaks the interview rules, which forbid comments about timing
It sounds too formal and will put the panel off
It signals you may not have prepared a structure and invites interruption

questions.hint: Own the shape of your answer.

items.title: L9: Handling escalating probes without contradicting yourself
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Civil Service Jobs interview guidance
items.body: Panels often probe in layers. The first question is the story; the next asks for your role, then your reasoning, then the evidence, then what you would change. This can feel like pressure, but it is the way panels check that an example is genuine and not rehearsed. The chief danger is inconsistency. If you embellish early, each probe forces you to invent more, and the details begin to conflict: a date, a team size, who made the final decision. Panels notice. The safest strategy is truthful preparation. For each story, write a one-page fact sheet with the dates, people involved, your exact actions, decisions that were not yours, the numbers you can support and what you learned. Then, in the interview, you can answer probes from memory because they are true. If you do not know a detail, say so and give your best estimate with a caveat. Never alter a detail to sound better. Layered probes also reveal how you think, so practise answering them aloud with a friend who is told to ask 'why' and 'what else' at each stage. When you reach the limit of what you remember, reflect on what you would do now: 'I did not measure it at the time; if I did this again I would track the time per case'. This turns a gap into evidence of learning. Finally, remember that probes are normal; a long series does not mean you are failing. It often means the panel wants to give a fair score and needs a little more.

questions.prompt: Why do panels probe in layers?

options.text: To move through the list of questions faster than a first answer allows
To make the candidate nervous so that their true character appears
To check that an example is genuine and to gather evidence against each criterion
To catch the candidate out in a mistake and mark them down

questions.hint: Layers fill gaps in the evidence.

questions.prompt: What is the main danger if you embellish an early detail?

options.text: The panel will award extra marks for the creativity shown in the answer
Later probes force more invention and details begin to conflict
The story will become too short to be scored under the criteria
The panel will stop probing once it hears a confident, detailed claim

questions.prompt: Which preparation tool best reduces the risk of contradiction?

options.text: A memorised script for each story, learned word for word and delivered in the same order every time
A list of impressive words to use in answers about leadership, drawn from the job advert
A single flexible story that you adapt for each question asked, whatever behaviour is tested
A one-page fact sheet for each story with dates, people, actions and numbers

questions.hint: True facts are easy to recall.

questions.prompt: You cannot remember a figure under probing. What is best?

options.text: State a precise number that sounds right, so that the panel sees confidence
Say you do not recall it exactly and give your best estimate with a caveat
Say the figure was not important and move on to the result
Change the subject quickly to another part of the story

questions.prompt: How can you turn a gap in your records into evidence?

options.text: Say what you would do differently now, such as tracking time per case
Argue that measuring results is unnecessary in a public service
Hide the gap by moving quickly on to a different part of the story
Ask the panel not to press you on results you did not record

questions.prompt: What does a long series of probes usually mean?

options.text: The panel has changed the criteria halfway through the interview
The panel is bored and is looking for a way to end the answer
The panel wants more evidence to give a fair score
The candidate is failing and the panel is giving them one last chance

questions.prompt: What is the best way to practise probes?

options.text: Write out every possible question in advance and memorise the answers
Ask a friend to keep asking 'why' and 'what else' after each answer
Re-read your notes silently until you can remember every detail
Practise only the opening of each answer, since probes are rare

questions.prompt: Your story says four people were in the team, but you later say five. What should you do?

options.text: Say nothing and hope nobody noticed
Change the earlier figure to match
Correct it plainly and carry on
Blame the interviewer's notes

questions.prompt: A panel member asks, 'What was the decision that was not yours?' What are they testing?

options.text: Whether you are willing to criticise the system in public
Whether you can name your manager and describe their role
Whether you disliked the decision and would have preferred another
Whether you can be honest about the limits of your role

questions.prompt: Which statement shows reflection under probing?

options.text: 'I did not track the delay at the time; if I repeated it, I would record it for each case.'
'The panel can check that from the records of the department if they want to see it.'
'I did not need to track it at the time, because the result was clear to everyone involved.'
'That detail was not important to the work that I did, so I did not note it down.'

items.title: L9: Evidencing outcomes rather than outputs
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Government Functional Standards and evaluation guidance (GOV.UK, HM Treasury Magenta Book)
items.body: An output is what you produce: a report, a training session, a process map. An outcome is the change it causes: faster decisions, fewer errors, better service, lower cost. Panels at higher grades look for outcomes, because the Civil Service is accountable for results, not activity. A candidate who says 'I produced a guide for new starters' has described an output. One who says 'I produced a guide, and new starters now reach full productivity about two weeks sooner, based on the team leader's records' has described an outcome. The HM Treasury Magenta Book, the government's guidance on evaluation, makes the same distinction between activities and the effects they are meant to have. When you cannot measure an outcome precisely, use a proxy and say it is a proxy: complaints, repeat contacts, time to complete, staff feedback, error rates, or user comments. Always attribute honestly. If other factors contributed, say 'the change coincided with a drop of about a third, although a seasonal fall may have contributed'. This level of care scores well because it shows objectivity. Think also about timescales: short-term outcomes (a week after the change), medium-term (three months) and unintended effects (did the change create work for another team?). A mature answer mentions at least one side effect or limit. Practise converting each of your stories from 'what I made' into 'what changed because of it', and rehearse the evidence for the change.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes an outcome rather than an output?

options.text: 'I drew up a process map and presented it to my manager.'
'I produced a guide for new starters and circulated it to the team.'
'I ran three training sessions for people in the office.'
'New starters now reach full productivity about two weeks sooner.'

questions.prompt: Why do higher-grade panels favour outcomes?

options.text: Outcomes are simpler to describe than the work that led to them
The Civil Service is accountable for results, not only for activity
Outputs are not allowed to be mentioned in a senior interview
Panels dislike any detail about the actions that candidates took

questions.prompt: What does the HM Treasury Magenta Book address?

options.text: How to evaluate government policies and programmes
How to calculate pay ranges for grades across government
How to run an interview panel so that scoring is fair
How to write a CV that meets the essential criteria for a grade

questions.hint: It is the government's evaluation guidance.

questions.prompt: You cannot measure an outcome directly. What is a sensible approach?

options.text: Claim a precise number so that the panel sees confidence in what you are saying
Say that outcomes cannot be measured in public service work, so none is offered
Use a clear proxy such as complaints or error rates and say it is a proxy
Leave out the result altogether, since it cannot be measured exactly by anyone

questions.prompt: Which wording shows honest attribution?

options.text: 'Complaints fell by about a third, though a seasonal drop may have contributed.'
'Complaints fell because of my work alone, and I take the credit for the whole change.'
'Complaints fell for reasons that were never really clear to anyone in the team.'
'Complaints fell and I take full credit for the change, as I led all of it.'

questions.prompt: What is an unintended effect of a change?

options.text: The time spent writing the report about the work
Extra work that the change creates for another team
The approval that the manager gave before work began
The planned saving that the change was meant to deliver

questions.prompt: Which is a medium-term outcome measure?

options.text: The title given to the project by the department
The number of slides used in the briefing for managers
The size of the meeting room used during the project
Error rates three months after the change

questions.prompt: Why mention a limit or side effect in your answer?

options.text: It avoids the need to give an actual result
It lengthens the answer so the panel asks fewer probes
It shows objectivity and mature judgement
It lowers the score, since panels prefer clean successes

questions.prompt: How should you rework a story that ends 'I ran training'?

options.text: Add more detail about the training slides and handouts
Remove the story and use a different example
Add what changed afterwards because of the training
Add the name of the trainer and where it took place

questions.prompt: Which proxy would best show a better service for the public?

options.text: More staff in the team handling the correspondence
Fewer repeat contacts from people chasing a reply
A longer procedure document explaining the process
More meetings held to discuss the service each week

items.title: L9: Interviewing for promotion from AO to EO
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Behaviours; Civil Service Jobs guidance
items.body: Moving from AO to EO changes what panels look for. At AO level, evidence of reliable, accurate work and good service is central. At EO level, panels expect more independence and ownership: you identify what needs doing, plan your own work, and take responsibility for results over a longer period. They also expect first signs of influence over others, even without management responsibility, such as guiding a new colleague, running a small process or coordinating a piece of work. When preparing, start with the EO behaviour descriptors and look for examples where you went beyond the task you were given. Good sources include covering for a manager, supporting an induction, running a rota, suggesting and testing a better way of working, or handling a difficult case independently. If you have not been given such opportunities, talk to your manager about stretch tasks; many departments also run development schemes. Internal candidates should avoid assuming their reputation will speak for itself: the panel scores what they hear. Be ready to explain what changed because of you. Explain also how you have prepared for the step up: courses, shadowing, or reading the EO job profile. A common weakness is describing a day-to-day task as an achievement ('I always process my cases accurately') which is good AO evidence but weak for EO. The test is whether the example shows you deciding, planning or influencing, rather than only completing. Finally, show you understand the wider context: why the team's work matters and how your role fits.

questions.prompt: What is the key shift in expectations from AO to EO?

options.text: Responsibility for a budget and for the pay of staff
A move from accuracy to speed as the main measure of success
Longer working hours and a willingness to cover for others
More independence, ownership and first signs of influence over others

questions.prompt: Which example is strongest evidence for an EO interview?

options.text: You saw that new starters were struggling and set up a simple induction checklist that the team adopted
You processed your cases accurately every week and had no complaints about your own work
You attended every team meeting and took the notes for your supervisor, who valued them
You followed your manager's instructions on a new task carefully and finished it early

questions.prompt: You have had few stretch opportunities. What is a sensible step?

options.text: Wait for the interview date to be announced and then collect examples
Ask your manager for stretch tasks and look at development schemes
Claim tasks that others did, since they were part of your team
Apply only after five years in the grade, whatever the evidence

questions.prompt: Why is 'I always process my cases accurately' weak for EO?

options.text: It mentions cases, which panels treat as confidential material from the department
Accuracy is not valued by panels at the higher grade, where speed counts more
It is too long to be scored fairly in a two-minute answer at interview
It describes completing a task rather than deciding, planning or influencing

questions.prompt: Internal candidates should avoid which assumption?

options.text: That their reputation will speak for itself
That feedback will be available after the interview
That they need examples to give the panel
That they will be asked questions about their current post

questions.prompt: Which detail shows preparation for the step up?

options.text: Mentioning how long you have served at the AO grade
Saying you are bored in your current role and want a change
Shadowing an EO and reading the EO job profile
Telling the panel that you are ambitious and ready to move up

questions.prompt: What question do panels implicitly ask of an example?

options.text: Was the task difficult for the candidate to complete, given the resources they had?
Was the task paid work, or was it done as a volunteer in another setting?
Did the candidate decide, plan or influence rather than just complete?
Was the candidate's manager present when the work was being done in the office?

questions.prompt: Which of these is an influence example without management responsibility?

options.text: Appointing a new starter to a vacant post
Guiding a new colleague through a complex process
Setting the team's budget for the coming year
Approving annual leave requests for the team

questions.hint: Influence does not need line management.

questions.prompt: Why show you understand the wider context of the team's work?

options.text: It shows you can see how your role contributes to outcomes
It avoids the need to describe the result
It lengthens the answer so that you can avoid the probes
It replaces the need for a real example

questions.prompt: What do departments' development schemes often offer?

options.text: A higher pay band for the length of the scheme
Automatic promotion on completing the scheme
Exemption from interviews for later promotions
Opportunities such as stretch tasks, shadowing or coaching

items.title: L9: Interviewing for HEO: delivering through others
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Behaviours (Leadership; Developing Self and Others); Civil Service Jobs guidance
items.body: HEO roles commonly involve managing people or workstreams, so panels look for evidence that you achieve results through others, not only by your own effort. Typical themes are setting clear expectations, delegating, supporting performance, giving feedback and managing workload fairly. For Leadership and Developing Self and Others, strong answers show that you recognised a need in a team member, agreed objectives, checked progress at sensible points and adapted your support. You should also show you can handle underperformance fairly: noticing early, speaking privately, listening for causes such as workload, unclear instructions or personal circumstances, agreeing specific improvements and following up, with advice from HR where needed. Remember that managing a person's performance involves confidentiality; describe the situation without naming them. Panels also expect planning across a team: allocating work according to skills and capacity, protecting quality and meeting deadlines. If you have not managed staff formally, use examples of leading a project, supervising students or volunteers, or mentoring a colleague, and make clear what authority you had. Common weaknesses include saying you do everything yourself because you can do it faster, which suggests an inability to delegate, and describing a manager role only by task lists. Another is failing to say how you knew the delegation worked. Show feedback loops: regular check-ins, shared tracking, and reviewing outcomes rather than simply trusting. Finally, show you look after your team's wellbeing and your own, because sustainable delivery matters.

questions.prompt: What do HEO panels especially look for in people-related examples?

options.text: Speed of personal output compared with the rest of the team
Results achieved through others, not just through your own effort
Length of service in the current grade
The number of meetings that the candidate chaired

questions.hint: Delivering through others is the shift.

questions.prompt: A candidate says 'I do the hard tasks myself because it is faster.' How may this be read?

options.text: As good time management under pressure
As evidence of teamwork with those around you
As strong leadership, since it ensures high quality
As a weakness in delegation

questions.prompt: Which sequence best handles early underperformance?

options.text: Reduce the person's work without discussing it with them, then wait for improvement to show
Wait until the annual review to bring it up, then agree a plan with them in writing
Notice early, speak privately, listen for causes, agree specific improvements, follow up
Raise it in the team meeting so everyone is aware of standards, then review the work after a month

questions.prompt: Why is it important to listen for causes of underperformance?

options.text: Workload, unclear instructions or personal circumstances may be involved
It avoids the need to set objectives for the person, which can be difficult
Causes are never relevant to how a manager handles performance, only the results
Panels expect sympathy to be shown towards the person in every single case

questions.prompt: When describing a performance conversation, what should you avoid?

options.text: Naming the individual
Describing what you learned
Describing your approach
Describing the outcome

questions.prompt: You have not line-managed staff. Which example is acceptable?

options.text: Avoiding the question and moving to a different example
Describing a manager's work as though it were your own
Leading a project or mentoring a colleague, making your authority clear
Pretending to have managed staff when you only worked alongside them

questions.prompt: Which shows a feedback loop after delegating?

options.text: Redoing the work yourself to make sure it is right
Trusting that the task was done and not checking again
Waiting for complaints before looking at the work
Regular check-ins and reviewing outcomes against agreed measures

questions.prompt: How should work be allocated across a team?

options.text: To the person who asks for it first
According to skills and capacity, protecting quality and deadlines
To the most senior person available
Evenly between everyone, whatever their skills or workload

questions.prompt: Why mention wellbeing in a leadership answer?

options.text: Sustainable delivery depends on looking after the team and yourself
It lengthens the answer so that the panel has fewer questions
Panels do not value wellbeing in leadership answers
It replaces the need to describe a result

questions.prompt: Describing a manager role only by task lists is weak because?

options.text: They take too long to read out and so use up the time for the result
It shows what you did rather than what you achieved through others
Task lists are not allowed in interview answers, and panels stop the candidate
They are too specific about what you did and leave out the context entirely

items.title: L9: SEO-level interviews: strategy, ambiguity and stakeholders
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Behaviours (Seeing the Big Picture; Making Effective Decisions; Leadership); Civil Service Jobs guidance
items.body: At SEO level, panels expect you to work with greater ambiguity and to look beyond your own team. Seeing the Big Picture is central: understanding how your area contributes to departmental and government priorities, anticipating changes, and using that to shape plans. Evidence includes adjusting your team's priorities after a policy change, linking operational data to strategic goals, or identifying a risk early. Making Effective Decisions at this level involves incomplete information, competing interests and risk. Strong answers show how you gathered evidence from several sources, consulted people with different views, weighed options and made a recommendation or decision, while being open about what was uncertain. Stakeholder management is a recurring theme: identifying who is affected, understanding their interests, building trust and handling disagreement. A useful method is to map stakeholders by influence and interest, tailor communication, and keep records of commitments. Panels also look for how you lead change: explaining the case for it, involving others, handling resistance and supporting people through it. Avoid describing change as a project plan only; the human side is part of the evidence. Another typical question is how you manage a risk or issue that crosses team boundaries. Describe how you escalated, who you involved and how you agreed ownership. Finally, show that you can disagree with senior colleagues constructively. Civil servants are expected to give honest, impartial advice even when it is unwelcome, and then to implement decisions lawfully once made.

questions.prompt: What does Seeing the Big Picture involve at SEO level?

options.text: Following instructions from above, passing them on accurately and reporting back on what was done
Reducing the workload of the team as far as possible while protecting its normal output
Focusing on your own team's tasks and deadlines, and reporting progress to your manager each week
Understanding how your area contributes to departmental and government priorities and anticipating change

questions.hint: It links local work to wider goals.

questions.prompt: Which example best shows Seeing the Big Picture?

options.text: Attending a conference on behalf of the team and sending round the slides afterwards
Completing a routine task ahead of the deadline and reporting it to your manager
Adjusting your team's priorities after a policy change affected demand
Reporting a monthly figure accurately to your manager before the end of the month

questions.prompt: What best characterises decisions at SEO level?

options.text: Little need to consult anyone outside the team
Incomplete information, competing interests and risk
Mainly routine choices that follow set procedure
Clear rules and a single obvious answer

questions.prompt: How should a strong answer treat uncertainty?

options.text: Be open about what was uncertain and how you handled it
Ask the panel to decide for you
Hide it so that you appear confident
Wait until it is resolved before deciding

questions.prompt: What is a useful method for stakeholders?

options.text: Ignore those who disagree with you
Contact only the most senior people involved
Map them by influence and interest and tailor communication
Treat every stakeholder in the same way

questions.prompt: A panel asks how you led change. Which element is essential?

options.text: Only the budget and how closely it was kept to throughout the period of the change
Only the project plan and timetable, with the milestones and the dates on which each was reached
Only the date on which the change was launched and the number of staff trained for it
The human side: explaining the case, involving others and handling resistance

questions.prompt: A risk crosses team boundaries. What should your answer include?

options.text: That you left it to the other team to sort out
That you solved it alone without telling anyone
How you escalated, who you involved and how ownership was agreed
That you ignored it because it was not your team's problem

questions.prompt: What is expected when you disagree with a senior colleague?

options.text: Work against the decision quietly once it is made, if you believe that it is the wrong one
Give honest, impartial advice constructively, then implement lawful decisions once made
Take the disagreement to the press if it cannot be resolved inside the department in time
Stay silent so that the decision is not delayed, then support whatever is decided in the end

questions.prompt: Why keep records of commitments to stakeholders?

options.text: It is required by law in every case
It reduces your workload for the next quarter
It avoids all disputes with stakeholders
It helps maintain trust and accountability

questions.prompt: Which of these shows early risk identification?

options.text: Spotting from operational data that demand would outstrip capacity and raising it with a plan
Reporting a problem to your manager after it has already happened and then explaining why
Waiting for the quarterly review to raise concerns, so that they can be put alongside other issues
Ignoring weak signals in the data, as they are unlikely to turn into actual problems

items.title: L9: Self-awareness and authenticity at senior grades
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Strengths; Civil Service Leadership Statement
items.body: Senior candidates are often asked about their strengths, development needs and style. Panels value self-awareness: an accurate view of what you do well, where you are less effective and how you manage that. Self-awareness is shown by specifics. Rather than 'I am a good communicator', say 'I am good at explaining technical issues to non-specialists; colleagues often ask me to review their briefings. I have learned that I sometimes over-explain in meetings, so I now prepare a one-sentence headline'. This names a strength, gives evidence, admits a related limit and shows a strategy. Avoid disguised strengths such as 'I care too much', which panels find evasive. Equally, avoid listing multiple weaknesses without remedies. Authenticity matters because senior roles require trust. Panels are alert to answers that sound like a script. Let your own voice and values show: why you value public service, what kind of leader you want to be, and examples of times you acted in line with those values when it was difficult. The Civil Service Leadership Statement sets out the expectations of leaders: to be inspiring, confident, empowering and respectful, among others. You can refer to it naturally but should anchor it in your own behaviour. Show also that you seek feedback: 360 feedback, trusted colleagues, mentors or coaching, and what you did with it. Finally, show resilience: leadership involves setbacks, and the panel wants to know how you recover, learn and keep your team steady.

questions.prompt: What is self-awareness in an interview?

options.text: Listing only your weaknesses and avoiding your strengths
An accurate view of strengths and limits, with a way of managing them
Listing only your strengths and leaving out your limits
Avoiding the question by moving to another topic

questions.prompt: Which answer best shows self-awareness?

options.text: 'I care too much about my work, which is probably my main weakness in the end.'
'I am a good communicator, and people I have worked with have told me so many times.'
'I have no real weaknesses that affect my work, as far as I am aware of at present.'
'I explain technical issues well; I sometimes over-explain, so I prepare a one-sentence headline.'

questions.prompt: Why is 'I care too much' weak?

options.text: It is a disguised strength and sounds evasive
It is too honest for a panel to accept
It is too technical for the panel to follow
It is too long for a strengths answer

questions.prompt: Which is also poor practice?

options.text: Saying how you improved after feedback
Naming one limit and a strategy to manage it
Listing several weaknesses with no remedies
Using an example to support a point

questions.prompt: Why does authenticity matter more at senior grades?

options.text: Senior staff must be informal and relaxed
Authenticity replaces the need for evidence
Panels dislike any structure in answers at senior grades
Senior roles rely on trust, and scripted answers undermine it

questions.prompt: How should you refer to the Civil Service Leadership Statement?

options.text: Avoiding it so that you do not sound rehearsed
Quoting it at length to show you know it
Naturally, anchoring it in your own behaviour
Reciting it as an opening to your answer

questions.prompt: What shows you seek feedback?

options.text: Using 360 feedback or a mentor and describing what you changed
Saying that you welcome feedback from anyone
Saying that you never need it as you are experienced
Asking the panel for feedback during the interview

questions.prompt: Why should a leadership answer mention resilience as well as achievement?

options.text: It avoids any probing about the results that you actually achieved in the post
Leadership involves setbacks, and panels want to know how you recover and steady others
It shortens the answer so that there is time for more questions at the end of the interview
Panels like to hear stories of failure for their own sake, so a leader should include one

questions.hint: Recovery and learning are part of leadership evidence.

questions.prompt: Which sounds more authentic?

options.text: A quote from a leadership book that you admire
A promise to be an inspiring leader if appointed
A list of values you hold, set out clearly
A specific story of acting on a value when it was difficult

questions.prompt: What do panels listen for beneath self-description?

options.text: Confident tone, which is the main indicator
Long, detailed sentences about each trait
Specific evidence that supports the claim
Strong adjectives that describe the candidate's character

items.title: L9: Giving credit and taking responsibility as a leader
items.source: Civil Service Leadership Statement; Civil Service Success Profiles: Leadership
items.body: A common challenge in leadership interviews is balancing credit and responsibility. Panels want to hear what you did, but they also expect leaders to give credit to their teams and to take responsibility when things go wrong. The wording signals your approach. Phrases such as 'my team delivered, and my part was...' show you can recognise others while still describing your contribution. When something fails, leaders take ownership: 'I had not made the priorities clear enough' rather than 'the team missed the deadline'. This is not self-blame; it is accepting accountability for the system you lead. Such answers also help the panel see how you create psychological safety, because staff who see their leader own mistakes are more likely to raise problems early. A strong answer includes what you did to put it right and what you changed, such as clearer objectives or earlier check-ins. Avoid two opposite errors. The first is claiming sole credit for a team's success, which suggests poor teamwork. The second is hiding behind the team on failure, which suggests weak accountability. Panels also check credit with questions such as 'What would your team say about you?' or 'Who else contributed?'. Prepare honest answers and, if possible, real examples of feedback from team members. It is also worth showing how you recognise good work: thanking people publicly, putting forward names for recognition, or giving others the chance to present to senior colleagues. These are concrete behaviours that show you develop others, not just direct them.

questions.prompt: Which phrasing best balances credit and contribution?

options.text: 'It just happened over the course of the year, with everybody contributing in their own way.'
'My team delivered it; my part was setting the priorities and clearing blockers.'
'I delivered it, and I want to be clear that the credit belongs to me for the result.'
'The team did it all, and I simply watched over it from a distance until it was done.'

questions.hint: Recognise others and state your part.

questions.prompt: A project missed its deadline. Which response shows ownership?

options.text: 'I had not made the priorities clear enough, so I reset them.'
'Another team let us down at a late stage in the process.'
'The deadline was unrealistic from the start, so it was always going to slip.'
'The team missed the deadline and I reported it to my manager.'

questions.prompt: What does owning mistakes help create?

options.text: A climate where staff raise problems early
More meetings to discuss each mistake in detail
Lower expectations of what staff can deliver
Less accountability for results across the team

questions.prompt: What is the error in claiming sole credit for team success?

options.text: It is too modest for a leadership interview
It suggests poor teamwork and weakens credibility
It shows accountability for the team's results
It reduces the risk of being probed

questions.prompt: What is the error in hiding behind the team on failure?

options.text: It shows learning from the failure
It is honest and builds trust
It suggests weak accountability
It shows teamwork and support for colleagues

questions.prompt: A panel asks 'What would your team say about you?' What should you do?

options.text: Say you do not know, since you have not asked them
Say only positive things to show that you get on with the team
Quote your own appraisal to the panel
Give an honest answer, ideally backed by real feedback

questions.hint: Evidence of how you are seen.

questions.prompt: Which action best shows recognising good work?

options.text: Asking them to work longer hours to repeat the success on the next project
Putting colleagues forward for recognition and letting them present to senior staff
Mentioning them by name in your own appraisal as valued members of your team
Thanking them privately, once, and moving on to the next task at hand

questions.prompt: After a failure, what should the answer include besides ownership?

options.text: What you did to put it right and what you changed
A promise that it will never happen again
A request for the panel's sympathy
A list of who was to blame for the failure

questions.prompt: Why do panels ask 'Who else contributed?'

options.text: To find another candidate to interview
To test your memory of colleagues' names
To check the balance between your claim and the facts
To lengthen the interview to fill the time

questions.prompt: Which phrase most signals accountability?

options.text: 'The system failed to warn us in time.'
'It was out of my hands by that stage.'
'Nobody told me it was behind.'
'I should have checked progress earlier.'

items.title: L9: Turning feedback into deliberate practice
items.source: Civil Service Jobs recruitment guidance; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Improvement in interviews comes from deliberate practice rather than repetition. Deliberate practice means focusing on one specific weakness at a time, practising it under realistic conditions, getting immediate feedback and repeating until it improves. Begin by analysing your feedback or a recorded mock: choose the single issue most likely to change your score, such as vague results. Set a measurable target: 'every answer includes one number or concrete change'. Practise using a bank of questions across behaviours, with a timer. Ask a reviewer to score your answers against the behaviour descriptors, using the same numerical scale as real panels, and to tell you which sentence earned or lost marks. Record yourself and review with a checklist: Did I say what I did? Is there a result? Does it match the grade? Is the length right? Rotate your focus each week: structure, then actions, then results, then delivery. Do not practise only your best story; test the weaker ones, and practise recovering from blanks, because that is what builds composure. Space your practice over weeks rather than the night before; memory and habits improve with spacing. In the final week, run one or two full mock interviews with someone unfamiliar, in a format like the real one (video if the real interview is on video). Keep a log of changes and review your scores over time to see if improvement is real. Avoid over-polishing: answers that are too rehearsed lose spontaneity, so practise with bullet notes rather than scripts.

questions.prompt: What best describes deliberate practice?

options.text: Focusing on one specific weakness, practising it with feedback, and repeating
Reading advice online and watching videos of interviews until you feel confident
Doing many full mock interviews in quick succession until the answers feel natural to you
Repeating your best story again and again until it sounds as polished as possible

questions.prompt: What should you choose first when analysing feedback?

options.text: All the issues at once, so that nothing is missed
The single issue most likely to change your score
The easiest issue, so you make quick progress
The issue the panel mentioned last in their comments

questions.prompt: Which target is measurable?

options.text: 'Sound better when speaking, especially in the opening of each answer.'
'Be less nervous before interviews by practising in the weeks beforehand.'
'Every answer includes one number or concrete change.'
'Be more confident in the room when the panel is looking at you.'

questions.prompt: What is the best form of reviewer feedback?

options.text: Comments on your appearance and body language only, from someone who was in the room
General encouragement and praise for the parts that went well, without detailed comment on each answer
A friendly chat about how the practice felt, followed by a score out of ten overall
Scoring against behaviour descriptors and showing which sentences earned or lost marks

questions.prompt: Why practise your weaker stories?

options.text: Because the weaker ones test your ability to recover and improve
The stronger ones are not needed once the weaker ones are done
It saves time to concentrate on stories that already work
Weak stories score highly if they are rehearsed

questions.prompt: Why space practice over several weeks?

options.text: It is a requirement of the competition
It removes nerves automatically
Memory and habits improve with spaced repetition
Panels notice early preparation and reward it

questions.prompt: What format should a final mock interview take?

options.text: Always written, as it is easier to mark
One like the real one, such as video if the real interview is on video
Always face to face, whatever the real interview will be
Always informal, so that you stay relaxed

questions.prompt: Who is the best person to run a final mock?

options.text: A family member who wants you to do well and will encourage you throughout
A close friend who knows your stories well and can prompt you with what you left out
Yourself, using a recording that you play back and mark against the criteria
Someone unfamiliar, who will not fill gaps from knowing you

questions.prompt: Why avoid over-polished scripts?

options.text: They always score low
They take too long
They are illegal
They lose spontaneity

questions.prompt: What does a log of changes help you check?

options.text: Whether the panel liked you at the interview
Whether improvement is real over time
Whether the job is the right one for you
Whether you can skip practice for the next application

items.title: L9: Raising concerns and the whistleblowing framework
items.source: Civil Service Code; Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998; Civil Service Commission
items.body: Leadership interviews sometimes ask what you would do if you saw wrongdoing, or you were asked to do something you believed was improper. The Civil Service Code says that if you are asked to act in a way that conflicts with the Code, or you see others doing so, you should report it. You can raise a concern with your line manager or another manager in your department, or with the department's nominated officer, who is appointed to receive such concerns and who should be independent of the line. If you are not satisfied with the response, you can report the matter to the Civil Service Commission, which is independent of government and can hear complaints under the Code. Separately, the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 gives legal protection to workers who make certain disclosures in the public interest, such as concerns about criminal offences, legal breaches, risks to health and safety, or concealment of wrongdoing, if they follow the right route. A strong answer shows proportion. You should check the facts first, as far as you properly can, avoid spreading rumours, keep records, and use the proper route before any external disclosure. Confidentiality matters, both for the person raising the concern and for others involved. Equally, a leader has a duty to respond properly when staff raise concerns with them: listen, record, protect the person from detriment and act or escalate. Strong answers avoid two extremes: ignoring the issue because it is awkward, or leaping to public disclosure. The panel is looking for sound judgement, courage and respect for process.

questions.prompt: If asked to act in a way that conflicts with the Civil Service Code, what does the Code say you should do?

options.text: Do it and say nothing
Ask a friend what to do
Report it
Quietly refuse without telling anyone

questions.prompt: Who is the department's nominated officer?

options.text: A person appointed to receive concerns under the Code
The head of HR in every department
The most junior member of staff in the team
The Permanent Secretary of the department

questions.prompt: If you are not satisfied with the response, to whom can you report?

options.text: Your trade union only
The Civil Service Commission
The newspapers
The nearest police station in every case

questions.prompt: What does the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 provide?

options.text: Immunity from every consequence of speaking out, whichever route is chosen by the worker
A pay rise for any worker who reports wrongdoing to a manager in good faith
A right to publish any information about an employer without any legal consequences
Legal protection for workers making certain public-interest disclosures

questions.hint: Protection if the proper route is followed.

questions.prompt: Which is a sensible first step on seeing possible wrongdoing?

options.text: Check the facts as far as you properly can and keep records
Post about it on social media so that it is investigated
Spread the word among colleagues to see whether they agree
Confront the person publicly in front of others

questions.prompt: Why use the proper route before external disclosure?

options.text: It is quicker than going straight outside, which can take several weeks to arrange
It avoids the need for any written record of what you saw or heard
It respects process and is usually required for protection
It keeps the matter secret from everyone, including those who should be told

questions.prompt: What should a leader do when a staff member raises a concern?

options.text: Tell others who raised it so that they can support them
Listen, record, protect them from detriment and act or escalate
Dismiss it unless there is proof already
Handle it privately without recording anything

questions.prompt: Why does confidentiality matter?

options.text: It is optional and applies only in some departments that choose to follow it
It avoids any inquiry into the matter, which would otherwise waste time
It protects both the person raising the concern and others involved
It speeds up investigations by limiting the number of people who know

questions.prompt: Which extremes should answers avoid?

options.text: Seeking advice from a manager or nominated officer
Using the nominated officer route for a concern
Checking the facts before acting
Ignoring the issue, or leaping to public disclosure

questions.prompt: Which quality does the panel look for in this question?

options.text: Judgement, courage and respect for process
Loyalty to colleagues above all other considerations
Speed in reporting the concern to the outside world
Silence until the matter has been closed

items.title: L9: Presentations for senior interviews: message, audience and challenge
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Communicating and Influencing; GOV.UK writing guidance
items.body: A senior presentation exercise tests your ability to communicate a clear message to a defined audience, usually in a short time, and to defend it under challenge. Start by clarifying the brief: who is the audience (a director, a minister's office, a delivery team), what decision or understanding they need, and how long you have. Then find your single key message, which should be a sentence you could say in a lift. Build the structure around it: the recommendation first, then three or fewer supporting points, each with evidence, followed by risks and next steps. This answer-first structure is often called the pyramid principle. Use plain language and avoid jargon unless the audience uses it; explain numbers by comparison ('about one in five') so that they are meaningful. Slides, if used, should carry one idea each and a headline that states the point, not just a topic label. Prepare for the questions: list the five most likely challenges, including cost, risk, evidence and who is affected, and prepare brief answers. When challenged, listen to the full question, acknowledge it, answer concisely and link back to your message. If you are asked something you cannot answer, say what you know, what you do not know and how you would find out. Do not become defensive when a panel member suggests an alternative; ask what would make it better and show your willingness to adapt. Finally, practise the first minute until it is fluent, because a clear start steadies the rest of the delivery.

questions.prompt: What should you clarify first with a presentation brief?

options.text: The font and layout to use for the slides
The panel's names and their job titles
Who the audience is, what they need, and how long you have
The colour scheme that the department prefers

questions.hint: Audience and purpose shape the content.

questions.prompt: What is meant by a key message in a presentation?

options.text: A single sentence you could say in a lift
A summary of every point you plan to cover
The title that appears on the first slide
The conclusion alone, left until the end of the talk

questions.hint: Focus the talk on one idea.

questions.prompt: What does the pyramid principle recommend?

options.text: Listing all the facts first, then the options
Leading with the recommendation, then supporting points with evidence
Beginning with the background and building to a recommendation
Ending with the recommendation only, after the evidence

questions.prompt: Which slide headline is best?

options.text: 'Overview of the project and its main stages for the panel'
'Background to the referral process and why it was set up'
'Waiting times in the referral service, 2021 to 2024'
'Early referral cuts waiting by a third'

questions.prompt: How can numbers be made meaningful?

options.text: By quoting figures to several decimal places
By removing the numbers and describing them in general terms
By placing them all in a table at the end
By comparison, such as 'about one in five'

questions.prompt: How should you prepare for questions?

options.text: List the likely challenges such as cost, risk, evidence and impact, and prepare brief answers
Wait to see what is asked on the day, and then answer each question as it comes up
Memorise your slides word for word so that you can repeat them if you are asked
Avoid questions by speaking for the full time, leaving none for the panel to use

questions.prompt: A panel member suggests an alternative. What is best?

options.text: Reject it, since you have already decided your recommendation
Say it was considered and move on to your next point
Ask what would make it better and show willingness to adapt
Ignore the suggestion and carry on

questions.prompt: You cannot answer a question. What is best?

options.text: Guess confidently so that you do not appear unprepared
Say what you know, what you do not and how you would find out
Refuse to answer questions outside your brief
Change the subject to a point you know well

questions.prompt: Why practise the first minute until fluent?

options.text: A clear start steadies the rest of the delivery
It hides weak content in the middle of the talk
It avoids questions at the end altogether
It shortens the talk so there is more time for questions

questions.prompt: Which of these is a weak slide for a senior presentation?

options.text: One idea, with a headline that states the point
A simple chart with a headline and a key figure
A key figure given with a comparison for context
Dense text under a title such as 'Background'

questions.hint: Slides should support, not carry, the talk.

items.title: L9: Using the Success Profiles elements in a promotion interview
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Civil Service Jobs guidance; Civil Service Recruitment Principles
items.body: A promotion interview is usually only one part of a wider assessment using the Success Profiles framework. The five elements are Behaviours, Strengths, Ability, Experience and Technical. Not all are used for every vacancy. Departments choose a combination that suits the role: an internal promotion might combine a CV or statement of suitability, an interview on behaviours and perhaps a presentation, while a technical post may add a skills test. Read the advert to see what will be assessed and how: it states which behaviours, whether there is a strengths element, and which Experience is required. Experience is typically assessed by sifting your CV or application against essential criteria, so it is worth ensuring the application evidences each one in clear terms. Ability is assessed through tests, such as numerical or verbal reasoning, often online, and requires practice under timed conditions. Technical elements assess professional skills and may use exercises. Where several elements are used, weightings may differ, and a low score in one may affect the total or lead to rejection if there is a minimum pass mark. Therefore avoid concentrating only on the interview; check each stage. For a promotion, panels may also expect evidence of performing at the higher grade, such as acting up, stretch projects or leading change. Be sure you can show how your evidence maps to the new grade, not simply a long record at the old one. Fairness requires that internal and external applicants are assessed on the same basis, so strong performance in your current role does not replace evidence in the process.

questions.prompt: Which are the five Success Profiles elements?

options.text: Leadership, Speed, Ability, Skills and Education
Behaviours, Strengths, Ability, Experience and Technical
Behaviours, Teamwork, Tests, Experience and Pay
Strengths, Qualifications, Interview, Technical and Fairness

questions.prompt: How are Experience criteria typically assessed?

options.text: By an interview alone, with no reference to your application
By an informal chat with the line manager
By sifting your application against the essential criteria
By a personality questionnaire completed online

questions.prompt: How is Ability typically assessed?

options.text: Through a presentation given to the panel
Through your CV and job history
Through tests such as numerical or verbal reasoning
Through your manager's opinion of your work

questions.prompt: Where do you find which elements will be used?

options.text: From colleagues who remember a similar competition
In the job advert and candidate information
From the department's website for new staff only
From the panel on the day of the interview

questions.prompt: Why should you not focus only on the interview?

options.text: Low scores at another stage may lead to rejection, especially with a minimum pass mark
Other stages are optional and candidates can skip them without any effect on the result
The interview is the only stage that is scored, and the other stages are for information
Other stages never affect the final outcome, whatever the weighting set out in the advert

questions.prompt: What does a promotion panel often look for?

options.text: Only formal qualifications held, since they are easy to compare across all candidates
Only your reputation among senior staff, which is collected before the interview takes place
Only length of service in the department, which is taken as a measure of experience
Evidence of performing at the higher grade, such as acting up or stretch projects

questions.prompt: Why does a long record at the old grade not suffice?

options.text: Long records are discounted by panels
It is against the rules to refer to past grades
The panel prefers staff who are new to the department
The panel must see evidence mapped to the new grade

questions.prompt: How are internal and external applicants assessed?

options.text: On the same basis against the same criteria
External applicants are given priority at each stage
Internal applicants skip some of the stages
Internal applicants are given priority at each stage

questions.prompt: What is a Technical element?

options.text: A test of typing speed and accuracy
A check on the equipment you will use
An assessment of professional skills, sometimes by exercise
A personality questionnaire about working style

questions.prompt: Where weightings differ, what follows?

options.text: Only the interview counts towards the total
Some stages may count more towards the total
Only the CV counts towards the total
All stages count equally in every case

items.title: L9: Learning from a promotion rejection
items.source: Civil Service Jobs recruitment guidance; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Not being promoted at the first attempt is common, and how you respond matters both for your next application and for your professional reputation. Begin by asking for feedback promptly, and from the right person: the recruitment team, the panel chair or your line manager if they were not on the panel. Ask specific questions: which behaviours scored lowest, what was missing from the evidence, and whether the gap was in content (what you had done) or delivery (how you described it). Thank the person who gives feedback; it encourages candid advice in the future. Resist the urge to rebut each point. Take time to reflect, and then summarise the themes in your own words. Next, check the evidence against the grade. Ask whether your examples demonstrated the scope, independence and influence expected, or whether they were pitched at your current grade. If the issue is content, plan to build the missing evidence, for instance by seeking a project, covering for a manager, or joining a cross-team group. If it is delivery, plan targeted practice. Talk to a sponsor or mentor who can advise on opportunities and who may notice gaps you cannot see. In your department, find out when the next opportunities arise and whether there is a talent or development process. Keep your performance high in the meantime, as people will notice how you handle disappointment. Finally, do not overcorrect by changing everything. Keep what worked and change what the feedback supports. If you reapply, you may mention what you have done since, briefly, which demonstrates learning.

questions.prompt: Who is a sensible person to ask for feedback after a rejection?

options.text: Another candidate who applied for the same post and was also unsuccessful this time
A stranger on a careers forum online who has been through similar competitions
The recruitment team or panel chair, or your line manager if not on the panel
The most senior person in the department, whether or not they were on the panel

questions.hint: Go to those who know the process.

questions.prompt: Which question is most useful to ask?

options.text: 'Who was given the job in the end, and what had they done to earn it?'
'Was the process fair to everyone who applied, including the external candidates?'
'Why did you not pick me for the post, when I have worked here for several years?'
Which behaviours scored lowest, and what was missing from the evidence?

questions.prompt: Why distinguish content from delivery?

options.text: Panels score only the content of an answer
Different gaps need different remedies
It shortens the plan you need to write
Panels score only the delivery of an answer

questions.prompt: Why thank the person who gave feedback?

options.text: It encourages candid advice in future
It improves your score if you reapply
It ends the matter, so no more follow-up is needed
It is required by the recruitment rules

questions.prompt: Why resist rebutting each point?

options.text: Panels never change scores after the event
Defensiveness closes off useful advice
Rebuttal is not permitted after an interview
It lengthens the process and delays the next vacancy

questions.prompt: If evidence was pitched at the current grade, what does this suggest?

options.text: You need a longer CV with more roles listed, so that the panel sees your range
You should stop applying for promotion at this grade until your next appraisal
You need examples that show higher-grade scope, independence and influence
You need a new line manager who will support you with the evidence you gather

questions.prompt: How can you build missing content evidence?

options.text: Wait for the next vacancy before collecting any evidence
Claim credit for work done by others in your team
Repeat the same tasks until they look more impressive
Seek a project, cover for a manager or join a cross-team group

questions.prompt: What can a mentor or sponsor offer?

options.text: Advice on opportunities and gaps you cannot see
A guaranteed role at the higher grade
Access to the panel's scores for your interview
A way to bypass the normal recruitment process

questions.prompt: Why not change everything after feedback?

options.text: Keep what worked and change what the feedback supports
Everything about the first attempt was wrong
Change is always better than keeping what you did before
Panels reward novelty in how answers are given

questions.prompt: What can you briefly mention if you reapply?

options.text: The score that you received last time
Your disappointment at the result of the first attempt
The mistakes you think the panel made
What you have done since to address the feedback
